analysis.one_liner: Bans making or selling semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition magazines.
analysis.headline: The Senate's assault weapons ban, introduced with 45 cosponsors, never received a committee or floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons and ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds. Guns people already owned would be grandfathered: they could keep them, store them under lock, and sell them only through a licensed dealer running a background check. Hunting rifles and shotguns — bolt, lever, and pump actions and a long list of named models — would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be people exposed to gun violence, since the weapons and high-capacity magazines covered by the ban are the types most often used in high-fatality mass shootings. Police, retired officers, and federal nuclear-security personnel would keep access to the weapons for their work. Current owners would keep the guns they already had, under new storage and transfer rules.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon or any ammunition magazine holding more than 10 rounds, cutting off future supply of these weapons.

Exempts nearly all traditional hunting and sporting guns — bolt, lever, pump, and slide actions, rimfire rifles, and hundreds of named models listed in Appendix A — so the ban targets a specific category rather than firearms generally.

Requires grandfathered assault weapons to be securely stored or kept on the owner's person so they cannot be accessed by people legally barred from having guns, and requires a licensed dealer to run a background check before any private sale or transfer of a grandfathered weapon.

Directs the Attorney General to keep a public record of every semiautomatic assault weapon used in a crime and report it annually to Congress, and to require serial numbers and manufacture dates on any large-capacity magazines still produced.
Lets state and local governments use federal Byrne Justice Assistance Grant funds to pay people who surrender banned weapons or magazines through buy-back programs.

analysis.who_pays: Firearm manufacturers and importers would lose the right to make or sell the AR-15, AK-pattern, and other listed rifles, pistols, and shotguns, plus magazines over 10 rounds — among the best-selling product lines in the industry. Gun dealers would lose those sales, and owners of grandfathered weapons would face new secure-storage duties and mandatory dealer background checks on transfers. Taxpayers would fund the buy-back compensation through federal grant money.

drawbacks.text: Grandfathering blunts the effect: weapons lawfully owned before enactment could be kept and even resold through dealers, so the large existing stock of these firearms and magazines would remain in circulation for decades. The ban cuts off future supply, not what is already out there.

The ban reaches possession, not just commerce, so a person found with a covered weapon would face federal criminal liability — and the definitions turn on attachments like pistol grips, threaded barrels, and barrel shrouds, which critics argue draws the line by gun cosmetics rather than function while functionally similar rifles on the Appendix A exemption list stay legal.

Compensating owners who surrender weapons through buy-backs would draw on federal Byrne JAG public-safety grant funds, a real cost to the treasury, and enforcement would fall on the ATF and federal prosecutors.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that studies of the earlier 1994–2004 federal ban reached mixed conclusions about how much it reduced gun violence, so the size of the public-safety payoff is genuinely uncertain — and the bill also carves out broad exceptions for police, retired officers, and nuclear-security personnel.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would shut off future production and sale of the weapon types most associated with high-fatality mass shootings while exempting most hunting and sporting firearms, a targeted trade. The costs are real but concentrated: lost revenue for gun makers and dealers, new storage and transfer duties for existing owners, and federal money for buy-backs. The main design weakness is grandfathering — it makes the ban a slow-motion policy whose benefits build over decades while today's stock of weapons stays in circulation, and the contested evidence from the earlier 1994 ban makes the payoff hard to promise.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with 45 cosponsors and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the Assault Weapons Ban of 2023 on January 23, 2023, joined by a long list of Democratic senators including Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and Judiciary Chair Richard Durbin.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded in its entire action history.

All 45 cosponsors were Democrats or the independent Bernie Sanders; not a single Republican senator signed on, leaving the bill far short of the 60 votes needed in the Senate to break a filibuster and reach a final vote.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still sitting in committee, so it expired without ever coming to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm manufacturers, importers, and dealers kept selling AR-15-pattern rifles, AK-pattern rifles, and high-capacity magazines, and current owners faced no new restrictions. Supporters of gun restrictions gained nothing; the country's laws stayed exactly as they were.

for.name: Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill, the latest version of the ban she had long championed.

for.name: Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, which was referred to the committee he chaired; the committee never took it up.

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no floor vote ever occurred while he led the Senate.

for.name: 42 other Democratic senators and Bernie Sanders (I-VT)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill 45 backers in the 100-member Senate.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Not one Republican senator cosponsored the bill, leaving it well short of the 60 votes needed to break a filibuster and get a final vote.

against.name: National Rifle Association and allied gun-rights groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal assault weapons bans and lobbied senators against them, as they have on every version since the 1990s.

against.name: Firearms industry and trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed the ban, which would outlaw their best-selling rifle lines and high-capacity magazines.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — 44 Democrats and one independent cosponsored, zero Republicans — and the bill never came to a vote in the Democratic-run Senate.

industries.note: The bill outlaws making, importing, or selling AR-15 and AK-pattern rifles, dozens of named pistols and shotguns, and any magazine over 10 rounds — among the industry's most popular product lines. The industry's sales interest runs directly against the bill's public-safety purpose.
Retailers would lose the banned product lines entirely, though the bill does route all private sales of grandfathered weapons through licensed dealers, who would run the required background checks.

Bolt-action, lever-action, pump, rimfire, and hundreds of named hunting rifles and shotguns are expressly exempted in Appendix A, so demand for their products could shift their way as the banned categories disappear.
